title: Clear Water, Thin Rescue: Kayak and Freedive the Albanian Riviera
subRegion: Albanian Riviera & Karaburun-Sazan Marine National Park

bestPeriod.window: Early June and the whole of September — warm sea, settled maestral afternoons, operators fully staffed, and none of the August traffic
bestPeriod.avoid: Late July–late August (the Riviera road becomes a single 60 km queue and beach prices triple) and November–April (most dive centres, kayak operators and boat services simply close)
bestPeriod.raw: Early June and the whole of September — warm sea, settled maestral afternoons, operators fully staffed, and none of the August traffic

accommodation.note: Guesthouse double ALL 4,500–7,000 (€46–€72)/night; Himarë and Dhërmi resort rooms ALL 9,000–16,000 (€92–€165) in August

food.note: Taverna main ALL 700–1,400 (€7–€14), grilled fish by weight ALL 2,500–4,500/kg (€26–€46), espresso ALL 100–150 (€1–€1.50)

transport.note: Hire car ALL 4,000–7,000 (€41–€72)/day plus fuel; Corfu–Sarandë ferry €25–€30 each way; airport transfers

activities.note: Karaburun-Sazan boat day ALL 3,500–6,000 (€36–€61), guided sea-kayak day ALL 5,000–8,000 (€51–€82), two-tank dive €60–€90, kayak/SUP hire ALL 2,000–3,500 (€20–€36)/day

profile.difficultyNote: 3/5 — sea-kayak days of 10–16 km and freediving on breath-hold, plus a steep 25-minute canyon descent to Gjipe with kit on your back

gatewayAirport: TIA Tirana Nënë Tereza — 2 h 30 to Vlorë, 4 h 15 to Himarë, 5 h to Sarandë. CFU Corfu plus the Corfu–Sarandë ferry (30–70 min) is often faster for the southern half of the trip.
summary: The Albanian Riviera has the clearest water on the Adriatic-Ionian arc and the least infrastructure to support you in it, and that combination is the entire character of this trip. You start at Vlorë for the one thing Albania protects properly — the Karaburun-Sazan Marine National Park, reachable only by boat, with the Haxhi Ali sea cave, the ancient graffiti-covered quarry at Grama Bay and a Cold War military island you can only land on with a licensed operator. Then you cross the Llogara Pass and drop onto the Riviera itself: Dhërmi, Jala, the canyon beach at Gjipe, Himarë, Porto Palermo's castle on its own isthmus, and finally the Ksamil islets in the far south. Days are structured around a simple wind fact — the sea is glass until roughly one in the afternoon, when the maestral fills, so the kayaking and freediving happen in the morning. What you will not find is a lifeguard, a marked channel, a functioning recompression chamber nearby, or a phone bill you can predict. Plan for that and this is one of the most rewarding weeks of water in Europe.

itinerary.title: Tirana to Vlorë, and a first look at Karaburun
itinerary.morning: Land at TIA, collect a hire car and drive south on the SH4/A2 to Vlorë — about 2 h 30. Take the coast road out to **Radhimë**, on the southern shore of Vlorë Bay, and check in near the dive centre rather than in Vlorë city.
itinerary.afternoon: Easy orientation swim and snorkel off Radhimë's shingle — flat, sheltered, and the calmest water you will meet all week. Register at **Albania Diving**: confirm your marine-park boat day, get sized for kit, and ask directly what the forecast is doing, because they will know before any app does.
itinerary.evening: Drive into Vlorë for dinner on the Lungomare — Restaurant Aragosta for fish, or any of the grill houses on the seafront where you point at the case and it is weighed in front of you.
itinerary.dayStats: TIA–Vlorë 150 km, 2 h 30 / Vlorë–Radhimë 12 km, 20 min / water 24–26°C in June / hire car ALL 4,000–7,000 (€41–€72)/day / visibility at Radhimë typically 12–20 m
itinerary.sleep: Guesthouse or small hotel at Radhimë

itinerary.title: Karaburun-Sazan: cave, quarry, military island
itinerary.morning: Full-day licensed boat out of Vlorë or Radhimë into the **Karaburun-Sazan Marine National Park** — leave at the operator's stated time, usually 09:00–10:30, because the maestral makes the afternoon return bumpy. First stop is normally the **Haxhi Ali cave**, a sea cave on the Karaburun cliffs large enough for the boat to enter, with a freshwater seep and a dramatic vaulted interior.
itinerary.afternoon: **Grama Bay** — a hidden inlet that was an ancient limestone quarry, its walls carved with more than a thousand inscriptions left by Greek, Roman, Byzantine and Venetian sailors over two millennia while they sheltered from the north wind. Swim, snorkel the quarry blocks on the seabed, then the landing on **Sazan**, the former military island with its bunkers and abandoned garrison — guided only, with the escorted route strictly enforced.
itinerary.evening: Back to Radhimë. Grilled fish and a bottle of Kallmet at your guesthouse; the drive to Vlorë after a full boat day is not worth it.
itinerary.dayStats: Marine park roughly 12,400 ha, declared 2010 / boat day ALL 3,500–6,000 (€36–€61) pp / Sazan landing licensed operators only, no overnight, parts off-limits / no road access to any of the park
itinerary.sleep: Guesthouse or small hotel at Radhimë

itinerary.title: Llogara Pass and the drop to Dhërmi
itinerary.morning: Drive the **Llogara Pass** — the SH8 climbs to just over 1,000 m through pine forest, then the Ionian appears 1,000 m below in a single turn. Stop at the pass for the view and, if you want a leg-stretch, walk part of the Cika ridge path.
itinerary.afternoon: Descend to **Dhërmi and Drymades**. The beach shelves steeply into deep water, so the snorkelling starts immediately: work the rocky spurs at either end of Drymades where the limestone drops in ledges and the visibility runs 20 m plus. Rent a kayak on the beach for a first low-commitment paddle north toward Palasë.
itinerary.evening: Sundown at one of the Drymades beach bars — Luani B is the long-standing one — then dinner in **Dhërmi village** on the hillside above, which is a different and much older place than the beach strip.
itinerary.dayStats: Radhimë–Dhërmi 55 km, 1 h 20 via Llogara / Llogara Pass summit ~1,027 m / maestral fills 12:00–13:00, 8–15 knots / kayak hire ALL 2,000–3,500 (€20–€36)/day / snorkelling visibility 20–30 m

itinerary.title: Sea kayak to Gjipe, and the canyon
itinerary.morning: The trip's centrepiece and the reason to be on the water by 08:00. Paddle south from **Jala** (or from Dhërmi, if you want the longer version) along the cliffs to **Gjipe**, a pebble beach wedged at the mouth of a limestone canyon with no road to it. The coast between is a wall of caves, arches and swim-throughs; go slowly and get in the water repeatedly. Go with a guide if you have not paddled an exposed coast before — there is no rescue service here.
itinerary.afternoon: Beach the kayaks and walk up into the **Gjipe canyon** itself — a narrowing gorge with 60–70 m walls that closes to a few metres wide. Then a long swim, and the paddle back before the maestral tops out. If you are not paddling, the alternative is the steep 25-minute walk down from the parking area on the road above.
itinerary.evening: Drive to **Himarë** and eat at Taverna Lefteri on the front, or at one of the grill houses on Spile beach. Himarë is the Riviera's most liveable base and where you should spend the rest of the week.
itinerary.dayStats: Jala–Gjipe by kayak roughly 4–5 km each way; Dhërmi–Gjipe roughly 8 km / guided kayak day ALL 5,000–8,000 (€51–€82) / Gjipe canyon walls 60–70 m / no road, no facilities, no rescue at Gjipe
itinerary.sleep: Rapo's Resort Hotel or a guesthouse, Himarë

itinerary.title: Freediving Himarë and the Porto Palermo submarine tunnel
itinerary.morning: Freediving or snorkelling session from **Livadhi** or the rocks below Himarë castle. This is limestone-reef water — walls, ledges, small caves, and 25 m visibility on a settled morning. Work with a buddy and a surface float; the drop-offs here go past 20 m within 50 m of shore, which is precisely why unsupervised freediving is a bad idea.
itinerary.afternoon: Drive 15 minutes south to **Porto Palermo**. Paddle or swim out to the **Ali Pasha fortress** on its low isthmus, then cross the bay to the **Cold War submarine tunnel** cut straight into the rock on the far shore — an abandoned Enver Hoxha-era pen big enough to take a submarine, and one of the strangest things on the Albanian coast. The bay is almost entirely enclosed, so it stays flat when the open coast is not.
itinerary.evening: Back in Himarë. Fish by the kilo at one of the Spile waterfront tavernas, and a raki you did not order.
itinerary.dayStats: Himarë–Porto Palermo 10 km, 15 min / fortress entry ALL 200–500 (€2–€5) / Porto Palermo bay flat in any maestral / freedive 3 mm suit June–September / two-tank dive €60–€90
itinerary.sleep: Rapo's Resort Hotel or a guesthouse, Himarë

itinerary.title: South to Ksamil and the islets
itinerary.morning: Drive south past Borsh and Lukovë to **Ksamil** — about 2 hours, on a road that has improved dramatically but still has blind bends and livestock. Ksamil's four small **islets** sit 200–400 m offshore in shallow turquoise water; paddle or swim out early, before the beach clubs put their loungers on the sand and the day boats arrive.
itinerary.afternoon: **Butrint National Park**, 15 minutes south — a UNESCO World Heritage site layering Greek theatre, Roman forum, early Christian baptistery and Venetian tower in one wooded peninsula between the lagoon and the sea. It is genuinely one of the best archaeological sites in the Mediterranean and almost nobody schedules enough time for it.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at the Mussel House on the Butrint lagoon — mussels farmed in the channel a hundred metres away, grilled and served by the kilo.
itinerary.dayStats: Himarë–Ksamil 80 km, 2 h / islets 200–400 m offshore, shallow sandy bottom / Butrint entry ALL 1,000–1,500 (€10–€15) / offshore easterly at Ksamil pushes toward the Corfu channel — do not paddle inflatables here
itinerary.sleep: Hotel in Ksamil or Bougainville Bay Resort, Sarandë

itinerary.title: Kakome or the Blue Eye, then out
itinerary.morning: One last piece of water: the boat or kayak run north from Sarandë to **Kakome Bay** and **Krorëz**, two of the least developed coves left on this coast, with the clearest water of the whole trip. Alternatively, if the sea is up, drive inland 30 minutes to the **Blue Eye (Syri i Kaltër)** — a karst spring pushing cold water up from a depth nobody has yet reached, which is the freshwater counterpoint to a week of salt.
itinerary.afternoon: Either the ferry from **Sarandë to Corfu** (30–70 minutes depending on vessel, roughly €25–€30) for a flight out of CFU, or the drive back north to Tirana, which takes 5 hours and should be started before 14:00.
itinerary.evening: If you are in Sarandë, eat on the Sarandë promenade and watch Corfu's lights come on across eight kilometres of water.
itinerary.dayStats: Sarandë–Kakome by boat roughly 12 km / Blue Eye entry ALL 200–300 (€2–€3) / Sarandë–Corfu ferry 30–70 min, €25–€30 / Sarandë–TIA 280 km, 5 h

accommodationStrategy.name: Radhimë guesthouse or small hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: Staying at Radhimë rather than in Vlorë city puts you ten minutes from the marine-park boat departures instead of forty, on flat sheltered water for evening swims, and away from Vlorë's traffic. Simple family-run rooms with a terrace and breakfast, and somewhere to hang a wetsuit. Roughly ALL 4,500–7,000 (€46–€72) double.

accommodationStrategy.name: Rapo's Resort Hotel
accommodationStrategy.description: The most established proper hotel in Himarë, on the bay with a pool and parking, walking distance from Spile beach and the kayak hire, and central enough for the Gjipe, Porto Palermo and Livadhi day trips without moving base. Roughly ALL 9,000–15,000 (€92–€155) double in season.

accommodationStrategy.name: Bougainville Bay Resort & Spa
accommodationStrategy.description: The comfortable last-night option in the south: proper facilities, secure parking, and close enough to both the Sarandë ferry terminal for a Corfu departure and to Butrint and Ksamil for the final day. Roughly ALL 12,000–20,000 (€120–€205) double.

logistics.connectivity: **Albania is not in the EU and EU "roam like at home" does not apply.** Roaming from EU SIMs can be expensive; a Western Balkans regional agreement and some voluntary EU–WB reductions have brought data prices down but coverage of those schemes varies by operator, so check yours before landing or you will get a four-figure bill. The reliable answer is a local prepaid SIM from **Vodafone Albania**, **One Albania** or **Eagle Mobile** at the airport — a data bundle costs a few hundred lek. Coverage is good along the coast road and in the towns, poor in the Gjipe canyon, on the Karaburun cliffs and in Grama Bay.
logistics.emergency: **112** is the number, with 127 for ambulance and 129 for police. There is no consumer coastguard hotline and no lifeguard network along the Riviera. Rescue response times on the coast road are slow and helicopter evacuation is not something to count on. **Assume no functioning recompression chamber within reach** — evacuation for a diving injury means Tirana or Corfu. Carry DAN Europe or equivalent dive/freedive cover explicitly including hyperbaric treatment and repatriation, and carry it in writing.
logistics.weather: The maestral is benign and predictable. The **veriu** northerly is the one that changes plans — it builds fast, closes the Karaburun boats and makes the west-facing beaches unlandable, and it can hold for three days. Watch Windy and, more usefully, ask the dive centre and the boat skippers, who read this coast better than any model. Thunderstorms over the Llogara ridge in late summer can put the pass in cloud with no visibility.
logistics.bookingWindows: August accommodation on the Riviera should be booked three months ahead and is expensive for what it is. Karaburun boat days and dive slots need 2–5 days in high season, and one flexible day held in reserve for weather. The Corfu–Sarandë ferry should be booked online a few days ahead in July–August, especially with a vehicle. Nothing else needs advance booking.
logistics.money: The currency is the **Albanian lek (ALL)**, not the euro, despite prices often being quoted in euros to tourists. Rate used here is roughly **1 EUR ≈ 98 ALL** — check it, the lek has appreciated notably in recent years and old guidebook figures are wrong. Cards are accepted in hotels, dive centres and larger restaurants; **beach bars, kayak hire, small tavernas, fortress entries and rural fuel stations are cash-only**. Draw lek from a bank ATM (Raiffeisen, Credins, Intesa) rather than the airport exchange, and avoid Euronet machines. Tipping is 5–10% and appreciated.
logistics.transportRules: Hire a car; there is no realistic alternative for a water-sports week. Albanian roads have improved but the Riviera road is narrow, unlit and shared with tour buses, and driving it after dark is genuinely unwise. Most Albanian rental companies **do not permit taking the car to Greece, North Macedonia or Kosovo** without a written cross-border authorisation and a green card — arrange it in advance if you plan a Corfu ferry with the vehicle. A UK or EU driving licence is accepted; an International Driving Permit is sometimes asked for. Fuel is widely available on the coast road, less so between Llogara and Borsh.
logistics.permits: Karaburun-Sazan requires a licensed operator in practice; **Sazan island landings are guided-only with a military escort and defined off-limits areas**. Anchoring on *Posidonia oceanica* is prohibited inside the park. Spearfishing on scuba is illegal. Drones are restricted over military installations, which explicitly includes Sazan and the Porto Palermo tunnel — do not fly there. Butrint and Porto Palermo charge modest entry fees. Removing archaeological material, including from the seabed at Grama Bay, is a criminal offence.
logistics.health: Tap water is not reliably potable on the Riviera — buy or filter. **Sea urchins on every limestone shelf** are the leading injury; wear reef shoes and carry a needle and antiseptic. Mauve stingers appear in patches. Sun exposure on open water here is severe and shade is scarce at Gjipe and Grama. There is a hospital in Vlorë and one in Sarandë; standards are variable and serious cases go to Tirana or, for those who can arrange it, Corfu.

proTips: Do everything on the water before 12:00. The maestral is gentle but reliable, and a coast with no rescue service is a coast you want to be off before the chop starts.
Book the Karaburun boat for your second day, not your last. If a veriu blows it out, you still have four days to reschedule; if you leave it to day six, you lose it.

Buy a local SIM at Tirana airport before you leave the terminal. Albania is outside EU roaming, the mobile bill is the single most common trip-ruining surprise, and a local data bundle costs less than a coffee in Dhërmi.
Take reef shoes and a second pair. The Riviera has almost no sand — it is limestone and urchins from Vlorë to Ksamil, and the local hospitals see the results daily.

Paddle to Gjipe rather than walking. The 25-minute path down from the road is fine but the sea route past the caves and arches between Jala and Gjipe is the best hour of the trip, and it puts you on the beach before the walkers.
Carry cash in lek, in small notes. Half the things you will want to do — a kayak, a fortress ticket, a beach lunch, a boat to Kakome — are cash-only, and the nearest ATM to Gjipe is 30 minutes away.
Ask the dive centre for the forecast, not the app. Karaburun's cliff wall generates local wind that no global model resolves, and the Radhimë skippers have been reading it for twenty years.

Go in September, not August. Water is at its warmest, the Riviera road is empty, prices halve, and the maestral is at its most reliable — August is the one month when the coast road can take three hours to cover 60 km.

Give Butrint a full three hours and go late. The site closes in the early evening, the tour buses leave by 15:00, and the light through the oaks over the Roman forum at that hour is the reason to have come south at all.

raw.Prevailing wind — the maestral, and the: The daily engine is the **maestral**, a northwest afternoon sea breeze that builds off the heated Ionian shore. It is light by Mediterranean standards: typically **8–15 knots, occasionally 18**, starting around 12:00–13:00, peaking 15:00–18:00 and collapsing near sunset. That gives you a reliable glassy morning window from first light to about 12:00, which is when every kayak, freedive and snorkel plan should sit. Two synoptic winds override it. The **veriu**, a strong northerly to north-northwesterly that funnels down the Ionian coast, is the one that shuts the Riviera down — it builds 1.5–2.5 m short-period swell onto the west-facing beaches, closes Gjipe and Jala for landing, and cancels the Karaburun boats outright; episodes typically last two to four days. The **juga** (sirocco), a humid southeasterly, brings haze, rain and long swell, and is more common in the shoulder seasons. Karaburun's own cliff wall creates violent local gusts and lee eddies that a small boat feels immediately.
raw.Launch spots and water, north to south: *Radhimë* (Vlorë Bay) — sheltered, shingle-and-rock, flat, the departure point for the marine park and the calmest launching water on the trip; all levels. *Dhërmi and Drymades* — long west-facing pebble beaches with a steep entry and a fast drop into deep blue; excellent snorkelling on the rocky spurs at both ends, exposed to any northwesterly swell, intermediate. *Jala (Jal)* — two small pebble coves separated by a rock nose, deep clear water, good freediving, but heavily developed with beach clubs in August. *Gjipe* — a pebble beach at the mouth of a limestone canyon, reachable by a steep 25-minute walk from the parking area above or by boat/kayak from Jala or Dhërmi; no facilities beyond a seasonal beach bar, no road, no rescue, and the single most beautiful piece of coast in the country. *Himarë (Spile and Livadhi)* — the practical base: sheltered, shingle, easy launching, kayak and SUP hire on the beach, all levels. *Porto Palermo* — an almost enclosed bay with the Ali Pasha fortress on its own isthmus and a Cold War submarine tunnel cut into the far shore; flat, protected, superb beginner kayaking. *Ksamil* — four small islets a 200–400 m paddle offshore, turquoise, shallow, sandy-bottomed, and packed in August. Bottom type throughout the Riviera is limestone and pebble, not sand: expect urchins.
raw.Karaburun-Sazan Marine National Park — t: Albania's only marine national park, declared in 2010, covering roughly 12,400 hectares around the Karaburun peninsula and Sazan island. **There is no road access to any of it.** You go by boat from **Vlorë port, Radhimë or Orikum**, and in practice only with a licensed tour operator or dive centre, because **Sazan island remains a military installation** — landings there are permitted only on guided, pre-authorised visits with an escort, parts of the island are off-limits, and overnight stays are not allowed. Inside the park, anchoring on *Posidonia oceanica* seagrass is prohibited, fishing is restricted, and spearfishing on scuba is illegal. A standard full-day speedboat tour from Vlorë runs roughly ALL 3,500–6,000 (€36–€61) per person and covers Haxhi Ali cave, the Karaburun cliffs and a Sazan landing; departures are typically mid-morning and the tours cancel outright in a veriu.
raw.Equipment hubs and certification: **Albania Diving at Radhimë** is the country's established operation — a PADI centre with multiple boats, full rental kit and the only outfit reliably running the Karaburun wrecks and cave sites, including the Italian submarine wreck at 30–35 m and the cathedral caves. Smaller seasonal dive and freedive operators appear at Himarë, Dhërmi and Sarandë between June and September, with SSI more common in the south than PADI; their season-to-season continuity is poor, so confirm before you travel. For sea kayaking, **Outdoor Albania** (Tirana) is the long-standing operator running guided multi-day Riviera paddles, and beach-front kayak and SUP hire is available at Himarë, Livadhi, Dhërmi and Ksamil. Indicative prices: discovery dive €40–€60; certified two-tank boat dive €60–€90; PADI Open Water €350–€450; full equipment rental €20–€30/day; sit-on-top kayak or SUP hire ALL 2,000–3,500 (€20–€36) per day; a guided kayak day with a certified guide ALL 5,000–8,000 (€51–€82). Storage is informal — most guesthouses will simply let you keep boards and fins in a back room.
raw.Tides and currents: The Ionian at this latitude is effectively **tideless: astronomical range is on the order of 0.2–0.3 m**, and wind set-up and barometric pressure move the waterline more than the moon does. Do not plan around tide state; there is nothing to plan around. What matters instead is **wind-driven surface drift and headland acceleration**. The Karaburun peninsula's western cliff face accelerates any northerly badly, and the gap between Karaburun and Sazan (the Sazan channel) can run a noticeable current in a strong wind. On the Riviera, the headlands at Cape Gjuhëz, the Gjipe nose and Cape Qefali all produce a sudden increase in wind and chop within a few hundred metres. Offshore-wind danger is genuine at Ksamil, where a light easterly off the mainland will quietly carry an inflatable or an inexperienced kayaker toward the Corfu channel and an international border.
raw.Sea safety — and the honest version: Water temperature: roughly 16–17°C in April, 19–20°C in May, 23–24°C in June, 25–26°C in July, 26–27°C in August, 24–25°C in September, 22°C in October. Visibility is exceptional, commonly **15–30 m** in summer. For freediving, a **3 mm suit is comfortable June–September, 5 mm in May and October**; snorkelling needs nothing but a rash vest in high summer. *Pelagia noctiluca* mauve stingers appear in patches after settled spells. **Sea urchins are everywhere** on the limestone — reef shoes are not optional, and this is the single most common injury on the Riviera. Now the part nobody writes down: **lifeguard coverage is effectively nil outside a handful of managed beach clubs, rescue boats are not stationed along the Riviera, mobile coverage drops in the canyons and on the Karaburun cliffs, and there is no reliably functioning recompression chamber on this coast.** A decompression incident means evacuation to Tirana or by ferry to Corfu. In practice: dive conservatively and well inside limits, never freedive without a trained buddy on the surface, carry DAN Europe or equivalent cover that explicitly includes hyperbaric treatment and repatriation, and treat every offshore paddle as fully self-supported. **Emergency 112** (also 127 ambulance, 129 police); maritime incidents route through 112 to the Albanian coast guard, and there is no consumer-facing coastguard hotline of the Italian or Greek kind.
raw.Boat and kayak logistics: Albania's recreational boating regulation is thin and inconsistently applied; there is no well-established licence-free horsepower culture, and small-boat rental to tourists is uncommon outside Ksamil and Sarandë. The practical reality is that you hire a boat *with* a skipper, or you paddle. Inside the marine park you must be with a licensed operator regardless. Anchoring on seagrass is prohibited. Harbour and marina infrastructure is limited: Orikum Marina is the only proper yacht marina on this coast, with Sarandë's port serving the Corfu ferries. Foreign-flagged yachts must clear in at Vlorë, Sarandë or Durrës.
raw.Weather-contingency plan: *Maestral too strong for open water:* Porto Palermo bay and Vlorë Bay at Radhimë stay flat when the open Riviera is choppy. *Veriu blowing (the trip-killer):* Karaburun boats and Gjipe landings are off — this is the day for the Llogara Pass and the Cika ridge walk, the Ali Pasha castle at Porto Palermo, Butrint's Roman and Venetian ruins near Sarandë, or the Blue Eye spring at Muzinë. *Juga with rain:* Gjirokastër, the Ottoman stone town 1 h 15 inland from Sarandë, is a genuinely great wet-weather day. *Sea too rough at Ksamil:* the Butrint lagoon and its mussel farms are entirely sheltered.

sources.verified: Karaburun-Sazan as Albania's only marine national park, declared in 2010, covering the Karaburun peninsula and Sazan island with boat-only access; the presence of Haxhi Ali cave as a boat-enterable sea cave and Grama Bay as an ancient quarry inlet on the Karaburun coast; anchoring restrictions over seagrass and fishing regulation inside the park; Albania Diving at Radhimë as the country's established PADI operation and effectively the only operator reliably running the Karaburun wreck and cave sites, with smaller seasonal outfits at Himarë and Sarandë and SSI more common in the south; indicative dive pricing (discovery €40–€60, two-tank €60–€90, Open Water €350–€450, kit €20–€30/day); summer visibility of 15–30 m and water temperature of 20–26°C June–October; the near-tideless Ionian; Albania's non-EU status for roaming purposes.
sources.confidenceNotes: **The Sazan island landing rules are the highest-risk item in this file.** Sazan is a former and partly current military site and the exact permission regime — whether landings require a named licensed operator, a permit, or only an escort — was not confirmed against an official Albanian source; verify with the National Agency of Protected Areas (AKZM) and with operators before publishing. Whether independent private boats may enter the marine park without a licensed operator is likewise unconfirmed. The absence of a functioning recompression chamber on the Albanian coast is stated on the basis of general reporting and must be checked with DAN Europe's chamber directory before publishing — it materially affects reader safety either way. All ALL/EUR conversions use **1 EUR ≈ 98 ALL** and must be re-checked; the lek has moved sharply in recent years. All prices are indicative for 2026 and unverified against published lists. Named accommodation (Rapo's Resort Hotel, Bougainville Bay Resort) and restaurants (Aragosta, Taverna Lefteri, Mussel House, Luani B) should be confirmed as still trading and open in the intended months. Outdoor Albania's current sea-kayak programme should be verified. Butrint, Porto Palermo and Blue Eye entry fees change annually. Albania's recreational boat-licence position was not verified against Albanian maritime regulation and is described here as an observed practical reality rather than a legal statement — confirm before publishing. Wind figures for the maestral and the veriu are qualitative and drawn from general Ionian climatology rather than a station record.
